document.title: Bin Ladin's Jihad: Political Context
document.authors: U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
document.note: [Confidential] Intelligence assessment of the political context behind bin Laden's terrorism. It concludes his extremism has found fertile ground in the Arab world, where perceptions of U.S. policies breed feelings of injustice and victimization. Few Arabs endorse his terrorism but many share some of his political sentiments.

INR issues intelligence assessment 'Bin Ladin's Jihad: Political Context', analyzing Arab public sympathy for bin Ladin's anti-US war; companion briefs on Kenya, Iraq and Iran/Afghanistan border buildup issued the same day.
actors: US Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research

events.description: East African embassy bombings referenced; media commentary after them argued such atrocities would not happen if US ceased unpopular policies.

relationships.detail: Bin Ladin's terrorism is characterized as rejecting increased US strategic and military domination of the Middle East, especially Saudi Arabia and the Gulf; Saudi religious leaders voice similar criticism of the US without violence.
relationships.quote: In Saudi Arabia, senior mainstream religious leaders have voiced criticisms of the United States in language very similar to that used by bin Ladin--without, however, the calls for violence.

relationships.detail: Bin Ladin launched his war against the United States at a time when US fortunes in the Middle East were at a low ebb.
relationships.quote: Usama bin Ladin has launched his war against the United States at a time when US fortunes in the Middle East generally are at a low ebb.

key_claims: Bin Ladin's terrorism is an extreme rejection of increased US strategic and military domination of the Middle East after the Gulf war.
Much of the moderate Arab public sees bin Ladin's violence as an understandable though extreme response to perceived US hostility.
Mainstream Saudi religious leaders voice criticisms of the US similar to bin Ladin's, without calling for violence.
The Arab 'double standard' argument over sanctions on Iraq and Libya versus Israel is central to perceptions of the US as hostile.
Few Arabs endorse bin Ladin's terrorism, but many share some of his political sentiments.
